svg.title: the framework guards what reaches the repository — clean commits and no secrets — the commit checks accept clean work and secrets never reach the repository
svg.text: the framework guards what reaches the repository — clean
Scenario: the commit checks accept clean work and secrets never reach the repository

g.text: Given a framework project has the commit hooks installed
A freshly initialized project already has commit checks turned on: init installed a
commit-msg hook, a script that runs before every commit message is accepted. The card proves
the hook is there, not what it says.
When a developer writes a conventional commit message
A conventional commit message follows a fixed pattern: a short type word, a colon, then a
plain instruction — like "feat: add login page".
Then the hooks accept it and let the commit through
The commit-msg hook calls commitlint, which accepts the message because it matches the
pattern.

text.tspan: git commit --allow-empty -m "feat: dogfood the commitlint hook"

g.text: When a developer writes a sloppy commit message
"sloppy" is not one of the allowed type words, so commitlint is about to reject it.
Then the hooks reject it with their own explanation
commitlint blocks the commit and lists exactly which rules it broke.
Given a project protected by the framework's secret scanner starts on a
clean feature branch
A freshly rendered project, committed once and checked out on its own feature branch:
nothing to report yet.
When the developer commits ordinary tracked, untracked and ignored
files
Ordinary work: one file gets committed, another sits in the project without being committed,
and a third is listed in .gitignore so git skips it. The scanner must leave all three alone.
Then the scan finds nothing to report
scan-branch runs clean and prints "No secrets detected in branch commits."
When the developer accidentally commits a private key to the branch
A fresh project (its own branch history): a fake RSA private key lands in a tracked file and
gets committed like any other change.
Then the scan blocks it and names the leak
scan-branch fails and prints "Gitleaks detected secrets in your branch commits!"
When the developer keeps a second secret out of the scan by gitignoring
the file it lives in
A fresh project again: the secret file is listed in .gitignore before it is ever committed,
so the scanner never even looks at it.
Then the scan passes silently, the ignored secret stays out of sight
scan-branch runs clean again and prints the same "No secrets detected in branch commits."
line — the gitignored key was never part of what it scanned.
